Constraint Satisfaction Problems

Backtracking, Heuristics, Constraint Propagation

Search that looks inside the problem instead of treating each state as a black box — and solves it far faster because of it.

Sudoku, exam timetables, colouring a map, assigning staff to shifts: these look like different problems, but they have one shape. Give every variable a value without breaking the rules. Because that shape is standard, we can reason about it in general — and cut away enormous parts of the search before ever visiting them.

Learning objectives

  • Define a CSP by its variables, domains, and constraints.
  • Trace backtracking search on a small CSP.
  • Apply the MRV, degree, and least-constraining-value heuristics.
  • Enforce node and arc consistency, and trace AC-3.
  • Use forward checking to detect failure early, and min-conflicts for large problems.

Key terms in this module

CSP say: Constraint Satisfaction Problem
A problem defined by variables, a domain of allowed values for each, and constraints saying which combinations are legal.
Variable
Something that needs a value: a region on a map, an exam, a Sudoku square.
Domain
The set of values a variable is allowed to take.
Constraint
A rule restricting the values that some variables can take together, e.g. "these two exams must not be in the same slot".
Hard constraint
A rule every solution must satisfy — the hard requirements of a performance measure (section 2.3). Preferences that can only be improved are handled by optimization instead (Module 4).
Assignment
A choice of values for some or all variables. Complete = every variable has a value. Consistent = no constraint is broken.
Backtracking search
Assign one variable at a time; when a variable has no legal value left, undo the last choice and try another.
MRV say: Minimum Remaining Values
Choose next the variable with the fewest legal values left. Also called the most-constrained-variable heuristic.
Degree heuristic
Tie-breaker for MRV: choose the variable involved in the most constraints with unassigned variables.
LCV say: Least Constraining Value
Try first the value that rules out the fewest options for the remaining variables.
Node consistency
Every value in a variable's domain satisfies that variable's own single-variable constraints.
Arc consistency
For every value of X there is at least one value of Y that works with it, for each constraint between X and Y.
AC-3
The standard algorithm that makes a whole CSP arc consistent by repeatedly checking pairs and removing impossible values.
Forward checking
After each assignment, delete the now-illegal values from the domains of the neighbouring variables. If a domain becomes empty, backtrack at once.
Min-conflicts
A local search method for CSPs: pick a variable that breaks a rule and give it the value that breaks the fewest rules.
Section 6.1

Same problem, many costumes

In Module 3 a state was a black box. The algorithm could only ask "is this the goal?" and "what are the neighbours?" It knew nothing about the structure inside a state.

A CSP opens the box. Once we know that a state is a set of variables with values, and that rules connect them, we can throw away huge parts of the search space using reasoning instead of exploration.

A CSP has three parts: a set of variables, a domain of allowed values for each variable, and a set of constraints saying which combinations of values are legal. A solution is a complete assignment that breaks no constraint.

Example: colouring a map

Colour the regions of a map so that no two neighbouring regions share a colour, using three colours only.

The constraint graph: variables are nodes, constraints are the lines between them.

The same three parts, three more times

  1. Sudoku

    Variables: the 81 squares. Domains: 1 to 9. Constraints: all different in each row, column, and 3×3 box.

  2. University exam timetable

    Variables: the exams. Domains: the available (room, time slot) pairs. Constraints: two exams sharing a student cannot share a slot; room capacity must be enough; some courses need a specific lab.

  3. Staff shifts in a hospital

    Variables: the shifts. Domains: the qualified staff. Constraints: nobody works two shifts in a row; each shift needs at least one senior nurse; weekly hour limits.

The hard requirements in a performance measure (section 2.3) become the constraints here: a solution must satisfy every one, which is why they are also called hard constraints. Preferences such as spreading exams evenly are not constraints; improving them is an optimization job (Module 4).

Why the path is irrelevant here

Nobody cares in which order you filled the Sudoku grid or the timetable — only the final grid matters. That makes CSPs close cousins of Module 4's local search. The difference is that a CSP has explicit rules, and those rules let us reason — we can prove a value is impossible without ever trying it, which is something plain local search can never do.

Constraints come in sizes. A unary constraint restricts one variable ("exam 12 cannot be on Sunday"). A binary constraint links two ("A and B must differ"). A global constraint links many at once — the most common being all-different, used in every row of a Sudoku.

6 min read

Section 6.2

Backtracking: guess, check, undo

The basic algorithm for CSPs is simple enough to write in ten lines.

  1. Pick an unassigned variable

    Any one, for now. We will improve this choice in the next section.

  2. Try a value from its domain

    Check it against the constraints with the variables already assigned.

  3. If it is legal, go deeper

    Move to the next variable.

  4. If nothing is legal, back up

    Undo the previous variable's value and try a different one. This is the backtrack.

def backtracking_search(csp, assignment={}):
    if len(assignment) == len(csp.variables):
        return assignment                       # complete and consistent

    var = select_unassigned_variable(csp, assignment)
    for value in order_domain_values(csp, var, assignment):
        if csp.is_consistent(var, value, assignment):
            assignment[var] = value
            result = backtracking_search(csp, assignment)
            if result is not None:
                return result
            del assignment[var]                 # undo and try the next value
    return None                                 # no value worked: backtrack
Filling a Sudoku with a pencil

You write a 4 in a square, continue, and three squares later you find a square where nothing fits. You rub out your last choice and try 7 instead. That is backtracking, and you already know how to do it.

i
Why the order of variables does not change the answer

In a path problem, the order of actions is part of the answer. In a CSP it is not: assigning exam A then exam B gives the same final timetable as B then A. So the search tree only needs to consider one variable at each level, not every possible order. That single observation reduces the tree from n! leaves to dn — still large, but enormously smaller.

Plain backtracking works, but it is slow, because it discovers failures late. The next two sections are the two ways to fix that: choose better, and reason earlier.

5 min read

Section 6.3

Three heuristics that change everything

Backtracking made two arbitrary choices: which variable to take next, and which value to try first. Choosing well can turn hours into milliseconds. The rules are counter-intuitive, so learn them as a pair.

Choosing the variable: take the hardest one first

MRV — Minimum Remaining Values. Choose the unassigned variable with the fewest legal values left.

Seating guests at a wedding

One guest can sit anywhere. Another can only sit at table 3 because of who he must avoid. Seat the difficult guest first. If you fill the easy places first, you may discover at the very end that there is nowhere left for him — and have to redo everything.

MRV finds failure early, which is exactly what you want: a branch that cannot work should be abandoned as soon as possible, not after twenty more assignments. When several variables tie, the degree heuristic breaks the tie: pick the one involved in the most constraints with variables that are still unassigned, because settling it simplifies the most of what remains.

Choosing the value: try the most flexible one first

LCV — Least Constraining Value. Try first the value that removes the fewest options from the neighbouring variables.

Why the two rules point in opposite directions

MRV picks the most constrained variable; LCV picks the least constraining value. That looks contradictory until you notice they answer different questions.

You must assign every variable, so for variables you want to hit the wall as early as possible — fail fast. But you only need one value per variable to work, so for values you want to keep as many doors open as possible — succeed easily. Fail fast on variables, stay flexible on values.

Check yourself

In the map above, region A has 3 colours available, B has 2, C has 1, and D has 3. Which variable does MRV pick, and why is that better than picking A?

Show answer

MRV picks C, with one value left. That choice is forced — there is nothing to guess — so taking it now either succeeds immediately or proves the branch is dead. Picking A first means guessing among three colours while a forced decision waits, and if C turns out to be impossible you will discover it only after wasting work on A.

Section 6.4

Constraint propagation: proving values impossible

Heuristics choose better. Propagation does something stronger: it removes values that cannot possibly appear in any solution, before the search even tries them.

Node consistency: the easy level

A variable is node consistent when every value in its domain satisfies its own unary constraints. If exam 12 cannot be on Sunday, delete all Sunday slots from its domain once, at the start, and never think about them again.

Arc consistency: the useful level

An arc X → Y is consistent when, for every value left in X's domain, there is at least one value in Y's domain that satisfies the constraint between them. If some value of X has no partner in Y, that value can never be part of a solution, so delete it.

Sudoku, the way you already play it

You look at a square and think: "this cannot be a 5, because there is already a 5 in the row." You did not try 5 and backtrack — you proved it impossible and crossed it out. That is arc consistency, and good Sudoku players spend more time doing this than guessing.

AC-3: doing it everywhere, until nothing changes

  1. Put every arc in a queue

    One arc for each direction of each binary constraint.

  2. Take an arc X → Y and clean X's domain

    Remove any value of X that has no possible partner in Y.

  3. If you removed something, wake the neighbours

    X's domain shrank, so every arc pointing into X must be checked again — a removal can cascade.

  4. Stop when the queue is empty

    If any domain became empty, this CSP has no solution from here — backtrack immediately.

i
Easy Sudoku puzzles are solved by AC-3 alone

Run arc consistency on an easy puzzle and the domains shrink to a single value each, with no searching at all. Harder puzzles need a guess, then propagation again, then perhaps another guess. That mixture — propagate, guess, propagate — is exactly how a modern CSP solver works.

Forward checking: propagation's cheap cousin

Full AC-3 after every assignment is expensive. Forward checking does one step only: when you assign a value to X, delete that value from the domains of X's immediate neighbours. If any neighbour's domain becomes empty, stop and backtrack now instead of ten levels later.

Forward checking

One step, cheap

  • Only checks the direct neighbours
  • Very fast per assignment
  • Misses failures that are two steps away
Arc consistency (AC-3)

Full propagation, stronger

  • Cascades through the whole graph
  • Detects failures much earlier
  • Costs more per assignment — worth it on hard problems

And for very large problems: min-conflicts

When there are thousands of variables, backtracking from an empty assignment is hopeless. Instead, start with a complete but broken assignment — everything placed, many rules violated — then repeat: pick a variable that is breaking a rule, and give it the value that breaks the fewest rules. This is local search from Module 4, applied to a CSP, and it solves problems like the million-queens arrangement in seconds.

8 min read

Section 6.5

Putting it together: the exam timetable

Take the problem you have met in every module of this course, and solve it properly this time.

Variables: the exams. Domains: the legal (room, day, slot) combinations. Constraints: no student has two exams at the same time; no room holds more students than it seats; large exams need large halls; some courses must be in a computer lab; no student has three exams on one day.

How a solver would actually run

  1. Clean the domains first

    Node consistency: remove from each exam every room too small for it, and every slot the department has blocked. This costs one pass and can remove most of the search space.

  2. Run arc consistency

    Some exams will now be forced to a single option before any guessing starts.

  3. Choose the hardest exam next (MRV)

    Usually the large exam that needs a big hall and clashes with many others. The degree heuristic breaks ties by picking the exam that shares students with the most unplaced exams.

  4. Choose the most flexible slot (LCV)

    Among the legal slots for that exam, take the one that leaves the most room for everything else.

  5. Forward check after each placement

    Delete that slot from every exam sharing a student, and backtrack the moment a domain empties.

  6. If the problem is huge, switch to min-conflicts

    Start from a full rough timetable and repair the clashes one by one.

Why constraints are a gift, not an obstacle

It feels natural to think more rules make a problem harder. In CSPs the opposite is often true. Every constraint lets the solver delete possibilities without trying them. A weakly constrained timetable has an enormous number of legal arrangements to wander through; a tightly constrained one collapses quickly to a few. The dangerous case is neither: it is the problem sitting exactly at the edge between "many solutions" and "none", which is where solvers work hardest.

Check yourself

A colleague says: "Our timetabling program is slow. Let us remove the rule about not giving a student three exams in one day — fewer rules should be faster." Is he right?

Show answer

Probably not, on two counts. First, removing a constraint enlarges the space of legal arrangements the solver must consider, and takes away a tool it was using to prune. Second, the rule exists to protect students, so removing it changes the product, not just the runtime. The real fixes are better propagation (arc consistency), better ordering (MRV and LCV), or switching to min-conflicts for a problem of this size.

Revision card

Module 6 cheat sheet

A CSP is three things

  • Variables — what needs a value
  • Domains — the values each may take
  • Constraints — which combinations are legal
  • Solution = complete assignment, no constraint broken
  • The path does not matter, only the final assignment

Constraint types

  • Unary — one variable ("not on Sunday")
  • Binary — two variables ("A ≠ B")
  • Global — many at once (all-different in a Sudoku row)

The three heuristics

  • MRV — pick the variable with the fewest values left (fail fast)
  • Degree — tie-break: most constraints with unassigned variables
  • LCV — try the value that rules out the least (stay flexible)
  • Remember: most constrained variable, least constraining value

Propagation levels

  • Node consistency — apply unary constraints once, at the start
  • Forward checking — after assigning X, clean the neighbours' domains
  • Arc consistency / AC-3 — cascade through the whole graph until stable
  • Empty domain at any point → backtrack immediately

AC-3 in four lines

  • Queue holds every arc (both directions)
  • For arc X→Y, remove values of X with no partner in Y
  • If X changed, re-add every arc pointing into X
  • Stop when the queue is empty; empty domain = no solution

Mistakes that cost marks

  • Swapping MRV and LCV — the variable is most constrained, the value least constraining
  • Saying arc consistency solves every CSP — it only prunes; hard problems still need search
  • Forgetting to re-check arcs pointing into a domain you just shrank
  • Treating a CSP as a path problem — the order of assignments is not part of the answer
  • Assuming more constraints always means a harder problem
